blocks.text: GOVT. T. ROMANA COLLEGE NOTES
ENGLISH
SEMESTER V & VI
SHORT NOTES & LONG NOTES
For use by students of Govt. T. Romana College only.

Folklore is the body of traditional beliefs, stories, customs, practices and expressive forms shared by a community. The syllabus introduces its basic concepts through Chapter 1 of Simon J. Bronner's Folklore: The Basics.

The English word 'folk-lore' was coined by William John Thoms in 1846 to replace the older phrase 'popular antiquities'. Today folklorists use it for traditional knowledge that is learned informally - by word of mouth, imitation and participation - rather than from schools or official institutions. It includes verbal forms (myths, legends, folktales, proverbs, riddles, songs), customary forms (festivals, rituals, games, beliefs) and material forms (houses, crafts, dress, food).

Bronner stresses that folklore is not only 'old' or 'rural'. A folk group is any group that shares at least one common factor - a village, a tribe, a profession, a college hostel, an online community - and every group creates its own traditions. Two key ideas are tradition (what is handed down) and variation (each telling changes slightly). Folklore therefore shows both continuity and creativity.

The prescribed European folktale presents a persecuted young woman whose fortunes change through supernatural assistance. It is useful for studying recurring folktale patterns such as hardship, transformation, reward and justice.

In the Grimms' version (Kinder- und Hausmärchen, 1812), Cinderella's dying mother tells her to be good and pious. The girl plants a hazel twig on her mother's grave and waters it with tears; it grows into a tree where a white bird grants her wishes. Her stepmother and two stepsisters treat her as a servant and set impossible tasks, such as picking lentils out of ashes, which helpful birds complete.

With dresses from the tree she attends a three-day festival and the prince falls in love. She leaves a golden slipper on the pitch-covered stairs. The stepsisters cut off a toe and a heel to fit the shoe, but birds reveal the blood. At the wedding, doves peck out the stepsisters' eyes. Compared with Perrault's gentler version (fairy godmother, pumpkin coach, glass slipper), the Grimms emphasise the dead mother's help, nature and harsh punishment of wrongdoers. Folklorists classify such stories as tale type ATU 510A, 'The Persecuted Heroine'.

sections.title: Little Red Riding Hood – Charles Perrault

blocks.text: The tale follows a young girl who encounters a dangerous wolf while visiting her grandmother. It works as a cautionary tale about danger, trust and disobedience.

Perrault's 'Le Petit Chaperon Rouge' appeared in his 'Histoires ou contes du temps passé' (1697). A girl in a red hood carries cakes and butter to her grandmother. She talks with a wolf in the wood and, not knowing it is dangerous, tells him where she is going. The wolf goes ahead, eats the grandmother, takes her place in bed and, after the famous exchange ('Grandmother, what big teeth you have!'), eats the girl too.

Unlike the later Grimm version, there is no huntsman and no rescue. Perrault ends with a verse moral warning young girls, especially well-bred ones, not to listen to strangers, and noting that the most dangerous 'wolves' are the smooth, charming ones. The tale is therefore a cautionary tale aimed at the courtly society of his time, with a clear sexual subtext about seduction.

sections.title: The Little Mermaid – Hans Christian Andersen

blocks.text: The tale centres on a mermaid who longs for another world and makes a costly sacrifice. It explores desire, transformation, suffering and the consequences of difficult choices.

Andersen published 'The Little Mermaid' in 1837. The youngest daughter of the sea king rescues a prince from a shipwreck and falls in love with him. She also learns that humans have an immortal soul while mermaids live three hundred years and then turn into sea foam. She goes to the sea witch, who gives her legs in exchange for her voice: her tongue is cut out and every step feels like walking on sharp knives.

If the prince marries another woman, she will die. He loves her only as a dear foundling and marries a princess he believes saved him. Her sisters offer a knife to kill the prince and regain her tail, but she refuses and throws herself into the sea. Instead of becoming foam she rises as a 'daughter of the air' who may earn a soul through good deeds. Unlike folk tales, this is a literary fairy tale with an author, a tragic ending and Christian ideas of sacrifice and salvation.
This Panchatantra tale uses animal characters to communicate practical wisdom and moral instruction. Students should focus on the conflict, deception and the way intelligence answers danger.

In the commonly told version, an old stork (or heron) that can no longer catch fish pretends to be sad and tells the creatures of a lake that the pond will soon dry up. He offers to carry the fish one by one to a larger lake, but actually eats each fish on a rock. When he finally carries the crab, the crab sees the pile of fish bones, grips the stork's neck with its claws and kills it, then returns to warn the others.

The tale belongs to the Panchatantra, a Sanskrit collection traditionally credited to Vishnu Sharma and composed to teach practical wisdom (niti) to young princes. Its lessons: do not trust someone simply because he speaks kindly, a greedy deceiver is destroyed by his own trick, and presence of mind can overcome a stronger enemy. Note the frame-story method, where tales are told inside other tales to illustrate a point.
A prescribed Panchatantra tale. It should be studied as Indian folklore with attention to generosity, moral values, narrative pattern and the lesson communicated through the story.

When preparing this tale, focus on how generosity is tested. In Indian moral tales, a king's greatness is often shown not by conquest but by willingness to give up wealth, comfort or even his own body for others, and this giving is rewarded or praised. Note the setting, the test or challenge, the king's response and the final outcome, and what the narrator wants the listener to learn.

In an answer, compare the king with other figures in the course: the clever crab and monkey survive by intelligence, while the generous king is admired for virtue. This shows that Indian folklore teaches both niti (worldly prudence) and dharma (righteous conduct). Always check names and details against the prescribed text, since many versions of such stories exist.
This Jataka tale uses wit and quick thinking in a dangerous situation. Like many animal tales, it teaches through simple action and a memorable moral situation.

A monkey living in a fruit tree by a river becomes friends with a crocodile and gives him fruit. The crocodile's wife decides that a monkey who eats such sweet fruit must have a sweet heart, and demands it. The crocodile invites the monkey to his home, carrying him on his back across the river, and in the middle of the water reveals his plan. The monkey calmly says he has left his heart hanging on the tree and must go back for it. Once ashore, he climbs to safety and mocks the foolish crocodile.

The Jataka tales are Buddhist stories of the former births of the Buddha (the Bodhisatta), who here appears as the wise monkey. The same story also appears in the Panchatantra as the frame of Book IV. Its lesson: keep calm in danger, and quick wit can save a weaker creature from a stronger one. It also warns about false friendship and greed.
A prescribed selection from Margaret L. Pachuau's Folklore from Mizoram. It should be studied as a Mizo traditional account of origins and for the cultural beliefs contained in the narrative.

Creation and origin narratives explain how the world, people, animals and customs came into being. In Mizo tradition such stories are linked with Pathian (the creator) and with other origin legends, the best known being the Chhinlung tradition, which says ancestors emerged from under a large rock. Read the prescribed text and note what existed first, who acts as creator, how humans and other beings appear and what explanations the tale gives for the way things are.

For examinations, explain the functions of such myths: they give a community its identity, explain the natural world, support beliefs and rituals, and are passed on orally across generations. Margaret L. Pachuau, who teaches at Mizoram University, collected and translated these narratives into English to preserve them and make them available to wider readers.
Chhura is the central figure of a prescribed Mizo folklore selection. Students should study the adventures, humour, characterisation and cultural values from the prescribed text.

Chhura is the most popular figure in Mizo folk narrative. He is a simple, sometimes foolish, sometimes surprisingly clever man whose adventures are told as short comic episodes. Many episodes involve his brother or companion Nahaia, who tries to cheat him; in some tales Chhura is the victim, in others he wins through luck or cunning. Listeners laugh at his mistakes but also sympathise with him.

Chhura is often studied as a trickster or 'wise fool' figure, comparable to similar characters in other cultures. His stories reflect everyday village life - jhum farming, hunting, food, family and community - and carry values such as hard work, sharing and wit. When answering, mention specific episodes from the prescribed text, Chhura's character traits and what the humour reveals about Mizo social life.
A prescribed selection from Folklore from Mizoram. Students should prepare its plot, characters, motifs, values and cultural context directly from the prescribed text.

Mauruangi is often called the Mizo Cinderella. In the commonly told version, the kind girl Mauruangi loses her mother, who is killed and continues to help her daughter in an animal or plant form after death. Mauruangi then suffers under a cruel stepmother and stepsister (Bingtei in many versions) but is finally rewarded, often through marriage to a chief's son, while the wrongdoers are punished.

This makes the tale an excellent comparison with Grimm's Cinderella: the persecuted heroine, the dead mother's supernatural help, jealousy within the family and justice at the end. Students should also point out what is distinctively Mizo - the village setting, food, work and the role of the chief - and confirm the exact sequence of events from the prescribed text.

Folklore consists of traditional stories, beliefs, customs and expressive practices transmitted within communities. It is important because it preserves cultural memory and gives insight into a community's beliefs and values.

The course deliberately brings together European, Indian and Mizo folklore. This allows students to notice both cultural differences and recurring features such as supernatural elements, moral lessons, cleverness, danger, transformation and justice.

Folklore has several important functions. William Bascom identified four: it entertains; it validates culture by justifying rituals and institutions; it educates, especially children, in an oral society; and it maintains conformity by praising acceptable behaviour and ridiculing or punishing bad behaviour. Folklore also gives a community a shared identity and connects present generations with ancestors.

The comparative approach in the course is important. Folklorists have found that similar tale types appear across distant cultures - for example, the Cinderella story exists in hundreds of versions from China to Europe and Mizoram. Possible explanations include migration and diffusion of stories along trade routes and similar human experiences producing similar narratives. Systems such as the Aarne-Thompson-Uther (ATU) tale type index help scholars compare these versions.

In a long answer, define folklore, outline its forms (verbal, customary and material), explain its functions, and illustrate with at least one European, one Indian and one Mizo tale from the syllabus. Conclude that folklore is a living tradition that still shapes identity today.

The syllabus prescribes Cinderella, Little Red Riding Hood and The Little Mermaid. Cinderella is structured around suffering, transformation and eventual reward. Little Red Riding Hood is a cautionary narrative involving danger and misplaced trust. The Little Mermaid centres on desire, sacrifice and transformation.

These tales are valuable not simply as children's stories but as examples of how folklore communicates social fears, wishes and values through memorable narrative patterns.

The three European tales come from different kinds of source. The Grimm brothers, Jacob and Wilhelm, collected tales they believed came from the German folk and published them in 1812-1815, editing them in later editions. Charles Perrault was a French courtier who rewrote oral tales in a polished style for aristocratic readers in 1697, adding verse morals. Hans Christian Andersen, a Danish writer, invented original literary fairy tales that use folktale style but have a personal author and often sad endings.

Common features include formulaic openings, repetition in threes, magical helpers or transformations, clear contrast between good and wicked characters and a moral lesson. Yet they differ in tone: the Grimms' Cinderella rewards virtue and punishes cruelty severely, Perrault's Red Riding Hood ends in death to frighten listeners, and Andersen's mermaid reaches spiritual reward through sacrifice rather than marriage.

These tales have often been interpreted psychologically (Bruno Bettelheim saw them as helping children deal with fears and growing up) and from a feminist point of view (critics note passive heroines whose value lies in beauty, obedience or silence). Mentioning such interpretations strengthens an answer.

The prescribed Indian selections are The Stork and the Crab, The Generous King and The Monkey's Heart. The first two are listed from the Panchatantra tradition, while The Monkey's Heart is from the Jataka tales.

Animal characters and compact plots allow such stories to communicate practical and moral wisdom. Students should examine how intelligence, behaviour, generosity, deception and consequences are represented in each prescribed tale.

India has one of the world's oldest written collections of folk narratives. The Panchatantra ('five books' or 'five treatises') is a Sanskrit collection, traditionally attributed to Vishnu Sharma, who used animal stories to teach statecraft and practical wisdom to three foolish princes. It travelled widely - into Persian, Arabic (Kalila wa Dimna) and European languages - and influenced fables everywhere. The Jataka tales are Buddhist stories of the Buddha's former births, used to teach moral virtues such as wisdom, compassion and generosity.

Features of these tales include animal characters who act like humans, a frame-story structure, short plots and a clearly stated moral, often in verse. In 'The Stork and the Crab', a deceiver is destroyed by a clever victim. In 'The Monkey's Heart', a weaker animal escapes by presence of mind. 'The Generous King' praises virtue and self-sacrifice.

In an essay, contrast niti (practical prudence for survival in a dangerous world) with dharma (moral goodness), and show that Indian folklore teaches both. Compare with European tales: magic is less central here, and intelligence and moral conduct carry the lesson.

The syllabus prescribes How Creation Came to Be, The Adventures of Chhura and Mauruangi from Margaret L. Pachuau's Folklore from Mizoram. These selections introduce students to Mizo traditional narratives and cultural memory.

For examination answers, students should connect the plot and characters with beliefs, humour, social values and cultural motifs actually present in the prescribed text. The Mizo selections are especially important because the course aims to understand the cultural psyche and traditional values expressed through folklore.

Mizo society had a rich oral tradition before the Mizo language was written in the Roman script by Christian missionaries in the 1890s. Stories, songs and sayings were passed down in homes and in the zawlbuk (the bachelors' dormitory, where young men learned discipline and village traditions). Collections like Pachuau's 'Folklore from Mizoram' record these narratives in English so that they are preserved and can be studied alongside world folklore.

The three selections show three types of narrative: a creation or origin myth ('How Creation Came to Be'), comic trickster or fool tales ('The Adventures of Chhura') and a wonder tale of a persecuted heroine ('Mauruangi'). Together they reflect values often associated with Mizo society, such as tlawmngaihna (selfless helpfulness and consideration for others), community life, respect for the chief and the importance of hard work in jhum cultivation.

For a long answer, describe each selection, explain what it reveals about traditional beliefs and social life, compare Mauruangi with Cinderella and Chhura with trickster figures elsewhere, and emphasise the value of preserving oral heritage in a changing society.

Literary criticism is the systematic interpretation, analysis and evaluation of literature. The background unit is prescribed from Chapter V of B. Prasad's A Background to the Study of English Literature.

Criticism has three main tasks: interpretation (explaining what a work means), analysis (examining how its parts - plot, character, language, form - work) and evaluation (judging its quality and value). Theory deals with general principles about literature, while practical criticism examines specific texts closely. The word comes from the Greek 'krites', meaning judge.

Prasad's background chapter traces English criticism from classical influences through the Renaissance (Sidney's 'Apology for Poetry'), the neoclassical age (Dryden, Pope, Johnson), Romantic criticism (Wordsworth, Coleridge) and Victorian criticism (Arnold) to the twentieth century (Eliot, Richards, New Criticism). Knowing this sequence helps place the three prescribed critics.
Aristotle examines poetry and drama, especially tragedy. Important ideas associated with Poetics include imitation or mimesis, plot, character and the emotional effect of tragedy.

Aristotle (384-322 BCE) wrote the Poetics around 335 BCE, partly in response to his teacher Plato, who had criticised poetry as an imitation of an imitation, twice removed from truth, and as dangerous because it stirs the emotions. Aristotle agreed that art is mimesis (imitation) but argued that imitation is natural to human beings, that we learn through it and take pleasure in it, and that poetry is more philosophical than history because it shows universal truths - what may happen - rather than particular facts.

The Poetics distinguishes art forms by their medium, objects and manner of imitation, and compares tragedy, comedy and epic. The surviving text deals mainly with tragedy; a second book on comedy is believed to have been lost.

Aristotle gives central importance to plot in tragedy. Tragic action should form a meaningful whole and produces the characteristic emotional response commonly discussed through pity, fear and catharsis.

Aristotle's definition: tragedy is an imitation of an action that is serious, complete and of a certain magnitude, in language embellished with pleasing ornament, in dramatic rather than narrative form, through incidents arousing pity and fear, bringing about the catharsis (purgation or clarification) of these emotions. He lists six parts: plot (mythos), character, thought, diction, song and spectacle, and calls plot 'the soul of tragedy'.

A good plot has a beginning, middle and end, and unity of action. Complex plots include peripeteia (reversal of fortune) and anagnorisis (recognition, a change from ignorance to knowledge), ideally together, as in Sophocles' Oedipus the King. The ideal tragic hero is a good but not perfect man of high status who falls because of hamartia - an error of judgement or tragic flaw - not because of wickedness. The unities of time and place were added later by Renaissance critics; Aristotle insisted only on unity of action.

sections.title: John Dryden – An Essay of Dramatic Poesy

blocks.text: Dryden presents literary criticism through a dialogue about drama. The essay considers ancient and modern writers and debates English and French dramatic practice.

Dryden published 'Of Dramatick Poesie, An Essay' in 1668. It is set on the day of a naval battle between the English and the Dutch in 1665, when four friends take a boat on the Thames and, as the sound of gunfire fades, discuss drama. Crites defends the ancients, Eugenius the moderns, Lisideius French drama and Neander ('new man', generally taken to represent Dryden himself) English drama.

Neander argues that English plays, with their variety, subplots and mixture of tragedy and comedy (tragicomedy), are livelier than regular French plays. He includes a famous tribute to Shakespeare as 'the man who of all modern, and perhaps ancient poets, had the largest and most comprehensive soul', and examines Ben Jonson's 'The Silent Woman'. The essay ends with a debate about rhyme versus blank verse in drama.
Dryden's criticism is comparative and practical. Rather than giving only rigid rules, he considers how drama works and weighs the strengths of different traditions.

Samuel Johnson called Dryden 'the father of English criticism'. He was a practising poet and dramatist, so his criticism comes from experience of writing. He respected classical authority but was not slavish; he judged works by their effect and by what pleases an audience. He defined a play as 'a just and lively image of human nature, representing its passions and humours, and the changes of fortune to which it is subject, for the delight and instruction of mankind'.

Key qualities: the dialogue form allows several views to be presented fairly; he is comparative and historical, realising that tastes change from age to age; he is flexible about the unities; and his clear, conversational prose helped create modern English critical prose. His prefaces (for example, to the 'Fables') contain further important criticism, including praise of Chaucer.
Wordsworth explains important principles of Romantic poetry. He argues for subjects drawn from common life and for poetic language closer to the language actually used by ordinary people.

Wordsworth and Coleridge published 'Lyrical Ballads' in 1798; Wordsworth added the Preface to the 1800 edition and expanded it in 1802. His aim was to choose 'incidents and situations from common life' and describe them 'in a selection of language really used by men', while throwing over them 'a certain colouring of imagination'. He chose humble and rustic life because there, he believed, the essential passions of the heart find a better soil and are expressed in plainer, more emphatic language.

He attacked the artificial 'poetic diction' of eighteenth-century verse, such as personified abstractions and fixed phrases, and argued that there is no essential difference between the language of prose and metrical composition. Metre, he said, adds pleasure and helps control strong emotion.
Wordsworth presents the poet as a person speaking to other people but possessing greater sensitivity and imaginative power. Poetry is closely connected with powerful feeling and reflection.

Wordsworth asks 'What is a Poet?' and answers: 'He is a man speaking to men', but one endowed with 'more lively sensibility, more enthusiasm and tenderness', a greater knowledge of human nature and a more comprehensive soul. The poet can feel and express emotions even when not directly provoked by real events. He calls poetry 'the breath and finer spirit of all knowledge' and the poet 'the rock of defence for human nature'.

His most famous definition: 'Poetry is the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings: it takes its origin from emotion recollected in tranquillity.' This means poetry begins with feeling, but the feeling is later contemplated calmly until a similar emotion is revived and shaped into a poem. So poetry combines feeling with thought; it is not simply uncontrolled emotion.

Literary criticism studies how literature works, what it means and how it may be evaluated. The syllabus moves historically from a general background to Aristotle, Dryden and Wordsworth.

This sequence introduces three important critical moments: classical criticism, neoclassical criticism and Romantic criticism. Students should understand not only individual ideas but also how views of literature and the writer change across these periods.

The three prescribed critics show how ideas about literature changed. Classical criticism (Aristotle) is mainly concerned with the work itself - its structure, unity and effect on the audience - and sees art as imitation of action. Neoclassical criticism (Dryden) values order, decorum, reason and imitation of classical models, but Dryden adapts rules to English taste. Romantic criticism (Wordsworth) moves attention to the poet's mind, emotions and imagination, and to the value of ordinary life and language.

M. H. Abrams in 'The Mirror and the Lamp' (1953) described this shift as a change from the mirror (art reflecting nature or life, the mimetic view) to the lamp (art as light projected from the poet's own mind, the expressive view). He also distinguished mimetic, pragmatic (focused on effect on audience), expressive and objective theories. Using this framework makes an answer on the nature and history of criticism stronger.

Also explain why criticism matters: it helps readers understand difficult works, sets standards of taste, preserves important works in the literary canon and connects literature with philosophy, society and history.

Aristotle's Poetics is one of the foundational works of Western literary criticism. It treats poetry as imitation and gives detailed attention to tragedy. Plot is especially important because tragedy represents an organised action rather than simply a collection of characters.

Concepts associated with Aristotelian tragedy include action, character, reversal, recognition, pity, fear and catharsis. His approach is analytical: he studies the structure and effect of successful dramatic works.

Plato's objection to poetry was twofold: it is an imitation far removed from reality (ideas), and it feeds the passions rather than reason, so poets should be banished from the ideal republic. Aristotle responds that imitation is a natural human instinct and source of learning, and that poetry shows universal truth. Through catharsis, tragedy does not inflame passions but purges or clarifies pity and fear, leaving the audience emotionally balanced. Thus the Poetics is a defence of poetry.

Plot is the most important element because tragedy imitates action and life, not persons in themselves; characters are revealed through what they do. The plot should be unified - every incident necessary and connected by probability or necessity - and of appropriate magnitude so that it can be grasped as a whole. Aristotle prefers complex plots with reversal and recognition, and says the incidents should arise from one another rather than from chance or a deus ex machina.

The ideal tragic hero is 'a man not eminently good and just, yet whose misfortune is brought about not by vice or depravity but by some error or frailty' (hamartia). The fall of a perfectly good man would be shocking, the fall of a villain would satisfy us but not move pity or fear. Evaluation: the Poetics established terms still used today, though it is fragmentary and based mainly on Greek drama; later critics turned its descriptions into rigid rules.

sections.title: Dryden's An Essay of Dramatic Poesy

blocks.text:
John Dryden's An Essay of Dramatic Poesy is written as a dialogue and discusses competing views about drama. It compares ancient and modern drama and considers English and French theatrical practice.

Dryden does not merely repeat classical rules. His criticism is comparative, balanced and attentive to actual literary practice. The essay is important in the development of English neoclassical criticism.

Structure of the debate: Crites praises the ancient Greeks and Romans for following the unities and imitating nature closely. Eugenius replies that the moderns have improved on the ancients, whose plots were often thin and whose characters lacked love interest. Lisideius praises French drama of his time for its regularity, decorum, single plot and avoidance of violence on stage. Neander defends English drama for its variety, liveliness, subplots, mixture of mirth and seriousness and its greater truth to the variety of human nature.

Neander's evaluation of English dramatists is a high point: Shakespeare is the greatest natural genius who needed 'not the spectacles of books to read nature'; Beaumont and Fletcher are praised for wit and gentlemen's conversation; Jonson is 'the most learned and judicious writer', whom Neander admires but does not love as he loves Shakespeare. He then analyses Jonson's 'The Silent Woman' as a regular English play, showing that English drama can also follow the rules when it chooses.

Importance: the essay shows a balanced, undogmatic neoclassical criticism; it treats literature historically, admitting that each age and nation has its own genius; it is the first major English work of comparative criticism; and its graceful prose made criticism a form of literature in its own right.

Wordsworth's Preface is a major statement of Romantic poetic theory. He rejects unnecessarily artificial poetic diction and argues that poetry can take subjects from ordinary life and use language closer to common speech.

He also emphasizes emotion, imagination and the special sensitivity of the poet. The Preface represents a shift away from strict neoclassical conventions toward a more personal and democratic conception of poetry.

Main arguments of the Preface: (1) The purpose of the poems is to trace 'the primary laws of our nature' in ordinary incidents. (2) Humble and rustic life is preferred because feelings there are simpler and more durable, and are connected with the permanent forms of nature. (3) The language of poetry should be a selection of the real language of men, purified of its defects, not artificial poetic diction. (4) There is no essential difference between the language of prose and of metrical composition. (5) Poetry is the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings, recollected in tranquillity. (6) The poet is a man speaking to men, with greater sensibility. (7) Poetry gives pleasure, and pleasure is the means through which it teaches truths about human nature.

Coleridge criticised parts of the theory in 'Biographia Literaria' (1817). He argued that rustic language is not necessarily purer, that the best parts of Wordsworth's own poetry do not use ordinary speech, and that there is an essential difference between poetic and prose language. Even so, he agreed with the rejection of false diction.

Significance: the Preface is often called the manifesto of English Romanticism. It moved the focus of criticism to the poet's mind and emotion, made ordinary people and nature worthy subjects and encouraged a more democratic, natural style. Its influence on later poetry, including modern free verse, has been enormous.

The background unit asks 'What is Pop Culture?' through John Storey's Chapter I. Popular culture concerns widely circulated cultural forms and raises debates about high and low culture, mass culture and cultural value.

John Storey's 'Cultural Theory and Popular Culture: An Introduction' opens by showing that 'popular culture' has no single meaning and offers several definitions: (1) culture that is widely favoured or well liked by many people (measured by sales or audiences); (2) the culture left over after deciding what is 'high culture' - therefore seen as inferior; (3) 'mass culture', commercially produced for passive consumers; (4) culture that originates from 'the people' themselves, like a folk culture; (5) following Gramsci, a site of struggle between the dominant groups' attempts to win consent (hegemony) and resistance from subordinate groups; and (6) a postmodern view in which the line between high and popular culture has collapsed.

Storey points out that the meaning of 'popular culture' always depends on what it is contrasted with. Studying popular culture seriously - as cultural studies has done since the 1950s with Raymond Williams, Richard Hoggart and Stuart Hall - challenges the idea that only canonical 'high' literature deserves analysis.
The song is prescribed as a Jamaican popular text. It deals with freedom, mental emancipation, oppression and the continuing need to overcome forms of domination.

Bob Marley recorded 'Redemption Song' with Bob Marley and the Wailers on the album 'Uprising' (1980). Unlike most of his reggae songs, it is performed by Marley alone with an acoustic guitar, in the style of a folk ballad. The opening lines recall the slave trade: 'Old pirates, yes, they rob I; / Sold I to the merchant ships'. The chorus calls it 'songs of freedom' and 'redemption songs'.

The most famous lines - 'Emancipate yourselves from mental slavery; / None but ourselves can free our minds' - are adapted from a 1937 speech by the Jamaican activist Marcus Garvey. The song argues that even after physical slavery and colonial rule end, people must free themselves from internalised inferiority. It also refers to the killing of prophets and fear of atomic energy. Marley knew he was seriously ill when he wrote it, which adds to its testament-like quality.

sections.title: Man in the Mirror – Michael Jackson

blocks.text: The song focuses on personal responsibility and social change. Its central idea is that improving the world must also involve examining and changing oneself.

'Man in the Mirror' was released on Michael Jackson's album 'Bad' (1987, single 1988). It was written by Siedah Garrett and Glen Ballard. The speaker sees poverty and suffering around him - children on the street without enough to eat, a 'broken heart' and 'a willow deeply scarred' - and realises he has been 'a victim of a selfish kind of love'.

The chorus states the key message: 'I'm starting with the man in the mirror, / I'm asking him to change his ways ... / If you wanna make the world a better place, / Take a look at yourself, and then make a change.' The mirror becomes a symbol of self-reflection. The song moves from personal confession to a gospel-choir climax, suggesting that individual change can become collective change. It also shows how popular music can communicate a moral or social message to a mass audience.
The prescribed South Korean popular song presents love through the idea of destiny and an almost biological or cosmic connection between two people.

'DNA' (2017) is the lead single of the BTS album 'Love Yourself: Her'. The speaker claims that he recognised his loved one at first sight, as if their meeting had been written in the universe and in their genes. Images include DNA, the Big Bang, galaxies, a 'blood type' and a 'religion' of love, mixing scientific vocabulary with ideas of fate and destiny.

The song is important in the study of popular culture as an example of K-pop's global spread through social media, fandom (the ARMY) and visual performance. Its lyrics combine Korean and English, showing cultural hybridity. Themes include destiny, the certainty of first love and youthful confidence. Consider how a love song uses science metaphorically and how global audiences consume songs whose language they may not fully understand.
The song responds to political violence and its human cost. Repetition and a forceful musical voice make it a protest against continuing cycles of conflict.

The Irish band The Cranberries released 'Zombie' in 1994 on the album 'No Need to Argue'. Singer Dolores O'Riordan wrote it in response to the 1993 IRA bombing in Warrington, England, which killed two children, Johnathan Ball and Tim Parry. The song refers to the long conflict in Northern Ireland ('the Troubles') and to 1916, the year of the Easter Rising.

The lines 'Another head hangs lowly, / Child is slowly taken' express grief for innocent victims, and the repeated cry 'In your head, in your head, zombie, zombie' suggests that people who continue violence in the name of old causes behave like zombies - mindless, unable to break free from history. The heavy guitar sound and O'Riordan's powerful voice, including her yodel-like cries, intensify the protest. The song shows how rock music can respond to political events.

sections.title: All Summer in a Day – Ray Bradbury

blocks.text: Bradbury's story is set on Venus, where the sun appears only briefly after years of rain. Margot's memory of sunlight and her classmates' cruelty create themes of jealousy, exclusion, regret and the value of experience.

Published in 1954, the story is set on Venus, where it rains constantly and the sun appears for only two hours every seven years. The children in a school are nine years old, so they were too young to remember the last sunshine - except Margot, who came from Ohio on Earth four years before and remembers the sun as 'like a penny' or 'a fire in the stove'. She is quiet, pale and withdrawn, and her parents may take her back to Earth.

The other children resent her memories and her difference. Led by William, they lock her in a closet just before the sun comes out. They rush outside and enjoy the sunlight, warmth and jungle for the brief hour, but when the rain returns they suddenly remember Margot and slowly unlock the door in shame. Bradbury uses science fiction to show childhood cruelty, envy, conformity, bullying of an outsider and the irreparable loss of a precious experience.

sections.title: What Matters More Than Your Talents – Jeff Bezos

blocks.text: The prescribed 2010 Princeton baccalaureate speech distinguishes natural gifts from choices. Its central argument is that character is shaped more deeply by the choices people make than by talents they happen to possess.

Bezos, founder of Amazon, gave this speech to the graduating class of Princeton University on 30 May 2010. He tells a story from when he was ten, travelling with his grandparents. His grandmother smoked, and he calculated aloud how many years of life she was losing. She began to cry. His grandfather took him aside and said, 'Jeff, one day you'll understand that it's harder to be kind than clever.'

From this he draws his message: 'cleverness is a gift, kindness is a choice. Gifts are easy - they're given after all. Choices can be hard.' He describes leaving a secure job to start Amazon as a choice of following passion over safety. He ends with a series of questions: will you follow dogma or be original, choose ease or adventure, wilt under criticism or follow your convictions, be clever at the expense of others or be kind? 'In the end, we are our choices.' As a text, note the use of personal anecdote, repetition and rhetorical questions in a speech.

The novel follows Nobody 'Bod' Owens, a child raised by the inhabitants of a graveyard after his family is killed. It combines fantasy, danger and growing up, and explores identity, belonging, courage and the movement from protection toward independence.

Neil Gaiman's novel (2008) won the Newbery Medal and the Carnegie Medal. A toddler escapes when a killer called the man Jack murders his family and crawls into a nearby graveyard. The ghosts Mr and Mrs Owens adopt him, and the mysterious Silas, who is neither living nor dead (implicitly a vampire), becomes his guardian. The boy is named Nobody Owens and is given the Freedom of the Graveyard, so he can see in the dark and fade from view.

Episodes include his friendship with the living girl Scarlett, the witch Liza Hempstock, adventures with ghouls and lessons from Miss Lupescu. Eventually the man Jack and his secret society, the Jacks of All Trades, return; Bod defeats them using the graveyard's powers. At fifteen he loses the ability to see ghosts and leaves to live in the world. Gaiman said the book was inspired by Kipling's 'The Jungle Book'. It is a coming-of-age story in which death and the past nourish life, but life must finally be lived among the living.

The paper introduces debates surrounding popular culture and the distinction between supposedly 'high' and 'low' cultural forms. John Storey's prescribed background provides the conceptual starting point.

The syllabus itself mixes songs, a short story, a public speech and a fantasy novel. This variety shows that popular literature and culture can be studied through forms that circulate widely and speak directly to contemporary audiences.

Debates about popular culture have a long history. Matthew Arnold ('Culture and Anarchy', 1869) defined culture as 'the best which has been thought and said' and feared the influence of mass society. F. R. Leavis and Q. D. Leavis in the 1930s attacked mass-produced novels, films and advertising. The Frankfurt School (Adorno and Horkheimer) described a 'culture industry' that produces standardised entertainment and makes people passive consumers.

Later critics took a more positive view. Raymond Williams said 'culture is ordinary' - a whole way of life - and the Birmingham Centre for Contemporary Cultural Studies under Stuart Hall studied how audiences actively interpret and resist media messages. Postmodern theory argues that the line between high and popular culture has blurred.

In an answer, show how the prescribed texts fit these debates: they are commercially successful and widely loved, but they also carry serious meanings about freedom, responsibility, violence, identity and growing up. Popular literature therefore deserves critical study because it reflects and shapes the values of large audiences.

Bob Marley's Redemption Song links freedom with emancipation of the mind. Michael Jackson's Man in the Mirror connects social improvement with personal responsibility. BTS's DNA presents love as a destined connection, while The Cranberries' Zombie protests against political violence.

Studying these works as texts allows students to examine theme, voice, repetition, imagery and social context alongside their status as popular music.

Each song comes from a different culture and genre: Jamaican reggae (Marley), American pop (Jackson), South Korean K-pop (BTS) and Irish alternative rock (The Cranberries). This shows the global circulation of popular culture. All four use repetition and a memorable chorus, a feature shared with oral poetry and ballads, which makes the message easy to remember and sing together.

Themes differ. 'Redemption Song' is postcolonial and political: freedom requires mental emancipation. 'Man in the Mirror' is moral: social change begins with personal change. 'DNA' is romantic and youthful: love as destiny expressed through scientific metaphors. 'Zombie' is a protest song mourning the victims of political violence in Northern Ireland. Literary features to discuss include the speaker's voice, imagery (mirror, chains, DNA, zombie), allusion (Marcus Garvey, 1916) and tone.

Also consider the debate on whether song lyrics are literature. Bob Dylan's Nobel Prize in Literature (2016) supports the view that they can be. However, lyrics are designed to be performed with music, voice and video, so a full analysis should mention performance as well as words.

sections.title: All Summer in a Day and Bezos's Speech

blocks.text:
Ray Bradbury's All Summer in a Day uses a science-fiction setting to present very human emotions. Margot remembers the sun while the other children do not, and their jealousy leads to an act of cruelty. Their later regret gives the story its emotional force.

Jeff Bezos's speech asks students to distinguish between gifts and choices. Talent may be given, but choices reveal and build character. Both texts therefore raise questions about human conduct and responsibility.

In 'All Summer in a Day', Bradbury contrasts Margot with the other children. She has a memory of the sun and refuses to join their games; she is different because of her experience, and the group punishes difference. The rain symbolises gloom and monotony; the sun symbolises joy, hope and life. The brief hour of sunlight and the image of the children 'like so many roses' and 'weeds' create poetic contrast. The ending, when they stand silent at the closet door, leaves readers to imagine their guilt and Margot's suffering.

Bezos's speech is a different genre - a commencement address - but it shares an interest in moral choice. His story of his grandmother contrasts cleverness (pointing out someone's faults) with kindness. The children in Bradbury's story choose cruelty, while Bezos urges his listeners to choose kindness. Both texts suggest that what we choose to do, especially towards vulnerable people, defines who we are.

As popular texts, both are accessible and widely read: the story often appears in school anthologies and was adapted for television, and the speech circulated widely online. Discuss techniques: Bradbury uses sensory imagery and irony, while Bezos uses anecdote, rhetorical questions, parallelism and a direct address to his audience.

Neil Gaiman's The Graveyard Book follows Bod Owens as he grows up among ghosts in a graveyard. The unusual setting combines fantasy with a coming-of-age story.

The graveyard is initially a place of safety and education, but Bod eventually has to face dangers beyond it. The novel explores belonging, family, identity, courage and the necessity of leaving protection behind in order to live independently.

Structure: each chapter covers a different stage of Bod's childhood, often at intervals of about two years, making it an episodic Bildungsroman. Silas teaches and protects him; Miss Lupescu, a werewolf (a 'Hound of God'), guards him when Silas is away; the dead of different centuries teach him history and letters. The living girl Scarlett and her family connect him to the outside world, and an attempt to attend a human school shows how hard it is for him to belong there.

Themes: (1) belonging and family - Bod's adoptive family of ghosts offers love as real as a blood family; (2) life and death - the dead are fixed in their time, while Bod can grow and change; Silas tells him that being alive means having potential; (3) courage and identity - Bod learns to face the man Jack, who wants to kill him because of a prophecy; (4) growing up - at the end the Freedom of the Graveyard fades and he must leave, with Silas's words that he should face life with 'his eyes and his heart wide open'.

As popular literature, the novel mixes horror, fantasy, humour and fairy-tale motifs, appealing to both children and adults. It shows how popular fiction can explore serious questions about mortality and growing up.
A report presents factual information in an organised form. It should have a clear purpose, relevant details, logical arrangement and concise language.

Format of a formal report: title; to/from/date (in a memorandum report); introduction stating purpose and terms of reference; method (how information was collected); findings, often with headings or numbered points; conclusions; recommendations; and signature with name and designation. Reports may be informational (presenting facts) or analytical (presenting facts with interpretation and recommendations).

Language: impersonal and objective (often passive voice, e.g. 'It was found that...'), past tense for events, precise figures and no unnecessary adjectives. Example topics: a report on a college sports week, a survey of drinking water facilities in a locality or a report on a blood donation camp.
A news report gives accurate information about an event. It normally answers basic questions such as what happened, where, when, who was involved and why or how it happened.

A news report usually begins with a headline (short, present tense, often without articles, e.g. 'Floods Hit Aizawl, 200 Families Displaced'), a byline and dateline (place and date) and a lead paragraph that answers the five Ws and one H: who, what, when, where, why and how. The remaining paragraphs follow the inverted pyramid structure - most important facts first, background and less important details later - so that an editor can cut from the bottom.

Use the third person, past tense for events, quotations from witnesses or officials with attribution, and a neutral tone. Avoid giving the writer's personal opinion; that belongs in an editorial or column.
An editorial presents an informed opinion or argument on an issue. It should state a clear position and support it with relevant reasoning.

An editorial is written by the editor or editorial board and represents the newspaper's official view; it is usually unsigned. A typical structure: (1) introduction presenting the issue and the paper's position; (2) background and evidence; (3) arguments supporting the position, with an acknowledgement and rebuttal of opposing views; (4) conclusion with a recommendation or call to action.

Types include editorials that explain, criticise, persuade or praise. The tone is serious, reasoned and persuasive rather than emotional or abusive. Example topics: road safety on hill roads, plastic pollution, youth unemployment, drug abuse or a new government policy.
Note-making reduces information into organised key points using headings, subheadings, abbreviations and a clear structure.

Steps: read the passage carefully to understand the main theme; identify the main ideas and important supporting points; give the notes a suitable title; arrange points under numbered headings and indented subheadings (1, 1.1, 1.2; a, b, c); use key words and phrases rather than full sentences; use recognisable abbreviations (e.g. govt., edu., dept., &, imp.) and list them in a key at the end.

Good notes are brief, logical and complete. Note-making is followed in examinations by writing a summary from the notes. It differs from note-taking, which is recording information while listening to a lecture.
An advertisement should attract attention, communicate essential information quickly and use language suited to its target audience.

Classified advertisements are short, placed under headings such as 'For Sale', 'To Let', 'Situations Vacant' or 'Lost and Found', paid by the number of words, so they use compact phrases and abbreviations and give essential details and contact information. Display advertisements are larger, use attractive headlines, slogans, pictures and different fonts, and are used for products, services, events and educational institutions.

The AIDA model is useful: attract Attention, create Interest, arouse Desire and prompt Action. Language should be lively, positive and suited to the target audience, but honest. Always include the essential information: what, where, when, price or terms and how to contact.
A job application is a formal letter expressing interest in a post and presenting relevant qualifications and experience.

Format: sender's address and date; receiver's designation and address; subject line ('Application for the post of ...'); salutation ('Sir/Madam'); body; complimentary close ('Yours faithfully'); signature and name; list of enclosures. The body usually has three parts: an opening stating the post applied for and the source of the advertisement; a middle paragraph highlighting relevant qualifications, experience and skills; and a closing paragraph expressing willingness for an interview and thanks.

A job application letter is often accompanied by a resume (or CV), so the letter should not repeat everything but should connect the applicant's strengths to the job requirements. Use formal, polite and confident language and keep it to one page.
A resume is a concise record of education, skills, experience and achievements prepared for academic or professional purposes.

A resume normally includes: name and contact details (phone, email, address); a career objective or profile statement; educational qualifications in reverse chronological order (most recent first) with institution, year and marks; skills (technical, language, computer); work experience or internships; achievements, awards and extracurricular activities; and references or a statement that references are available. Personal details such as date of birth are sometimes included in India but are optional.

A resume (one to two pages) is shorter than a curriculum vitae, which is a fuller record often used for academic posts. Use bullet points, consistent formatting, action verbs (organised, managed, designed) and make sure all facts are accurate and verifiable.
An abstract is a brief statement of the purpose, main content and findings or argument of a longer academic work.

An abstract typically has 150-300 words and appears at the beginning of a research paper, dissertation or conference paper. It answers four questions: what was the purpose or research problem, how was it studied (method), what were the main findings and what are the conclusions or implications. It is followed by keywords that help indexing.

Types: a descriptive abstract summarises what the work covers without giving results, while an informative abstract gives the results and conclusions as well. An abstract must stand alone, use no references or abbreviations without explanation and contain no information that is not in the main work.
A summary gives the central ideas of a longer text in a shorter form without unnecessary detail.

Steps in writing a summary (précis): read the original text twice; underline the main ideas; leave out examples, repetitions, illustrations and minor details; write the ideas in your own words in a connected paragraph; and check that the summary is about one-third the length of the original, or the length required. A summary should be objective - do not add your own opinions or new information - and should use the third person and reported speech.
Give the summary a suitable title if asked. Summary writing is useful for revision, academic writing and professional communication, where busy readers need the essence of a long document.
A notice communicates brief official information to a particular group and should clearly state the event, date, time, place and necessary instructions.

Format: the name of the institution or organisation at the top; the word NOTICE; date; a clear heading or title; the body (what, when, where, who should attend, any special instructions or contact person); and the name, designation and signature of the issuing authority. It is often written within a box in examinations and is usually about 50 words.

Language should be formal, brief and in the third person or passive voice (e.g. 'All students are informed that...'). Notices are displayed on notice boards or published in newspapers, so the heading must catch attention and the information must be complete and unambiguous.
An agenda is the ordered list of matters to be discussed at a meeting.

An agenda is circulated to members before a meeting, along with the notice of the meeting, so that they can prepare. It usually includes the name of the organisation; the date, time and venue of the meeting; and numbered items, typically: (1) welcome and apologies for absence; (2) confirmation of the minutes of the previous meeting; (3) matters arising from the minutes; (4) specific items for discussion; (5) any other business (AOB) with the chair's permission; and (6) date of the next meeting.
A good agenda keeps the meeting focused and prevents important matters from being forgotten. It should be clear, brief and arranged in a logical order of priority.
Minutes are the official written record of the important proceedings and decisions of a meeting.

Minutes record the name of the organisation, the type of meeting, date, time and venue; the names of the chairperson and members present and absent; and, item by item following the agenda, a brief account of discussion, resolutions passed and decisions taken, often with the name of the person responsible for action. They end with the time the meeting closed and signatures of the secretary and chairperson.

Minutes are written in the past tense, in reported speech, in a formal and impartial style. They are read and confirmed at the next meeting and become an official, sometimes legal, record. Types include verbatim minutes (word for word), narrative minutes (summary of discussion) and resolution minutes (only decisions).

sections.title: Report, News Report and Editorial Writing

blocks.text:
Report writing requires accuracy, clarity and organisation. A news report should give essential facts promptly and avoid unnecessary personal opinion. An editorial, in contrast, presents a reasoned viewpoint on an issue.

Students should therefore distinguish factual reporting from argumentative writing. In both forms, a clear structure and appropriate language are essential.

A report is a structured document prepared for a particular reader, usually to record an event or investigation and often to make recommendations. A newspaper report is written for the general public about a recent event. An editorial argues a position on a public issue. All three require planning: collecting facts, organising them logically and choosing an appropriate tone.

Differences: a report uses headings, findings and recommendations and an objective tone; a news report uses headline, dateline, lead and the inverted pyramid, and quotes sources; an editorial uses an argumentative structure (issue, position, evidence, counter-argument, conclusion) and persuasive language. Facts in a news report must be verified; an editorial must be fair and reasoned even when it is strongly critical.

Common errors include mixing opinion with news, burying the main point, using too much emotional language and leaving out essential details such as date and place. In examinations, follow the required format and word limit and give a suitable heading.

Note-making identifies the main ideas of a text and arranges them under headings and subheadings. Good notes are brief but meaningful and make later revision easier.

Advertisement writing requires economy of language and attention to audience. Essential details must be immediately visible, while the wording should attract interest without becoming confusing.

Note-making is a study skill and a professional skill. Notes are useful for revision, for preparing speeches or reports and for summarising long documents. The standard format has a title, numbered main headings, indented subheadings and sub-subheadings, key words rather than complete sentences and a list of abbreviations. Clear visual layout shows how ideas are related.

Advertisement writing is a form of persuasive communication. Classified advertisements are economical and factual; display advertisements are designed creatively with headlines, slogans, images and white space. The AIDA model (attention, interest, desire, action) helps structure a display advertisement. Effective advertisements identify the target audience, highlight unique features or benefits and include contact information.

Ethical issues are also important: advertisements should not mislead or make false claims. In India, the Advertising Standards Council of India (ASCI) sets voluntary standards, and the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 addresses misleading advertisements.

A job application should be formal, specific and relevant to the advertised position. It normally introduces the applicant and draws attention to suitable qualifications and experience.

A resume presents this information in a compact structured format. Typical sections include contact information, education, skills, experience and achievements. Accuracy and neat presentation are important.

Applying for a job involves a cover letter (application) and a resume. The letter is a formal introduction addressed to a specific person or designation. It identifies the job and where it was advertised, briefly connects the applicant's qualifications and experience to the job requirements and requests an interview. It should be one page and free from errors.

Resumes can be chronological (listing education and experience in reverse order of time), functional (organised by skills, useful for those with little experience) or combination. Employers often spend only a short time on each resume, so key information must be easy to find. Use headings, bullet points and action verbs, quantify achievements where possible and tailor the resume to the job.

Common mistakes: spelling errors, unprofessional email addresses, irrelevant personal details, exaggeration or false claims and inconsistent formatting. The applicant should keep copies of certificates ready and list them as enclosures.

sections.title: Abstract, Summary, Notice, Agenda and Minutes

blocks.text:
An abstract condenses the purpose and major content of academic work, while a summary restates the main ideas of a longer text. Both require selection of essential information.

A notice gives concise official information. An agenda lists items for a meeting in order, while minutes record the proceedings and decisions after the meeting. These forms are important in academic and professional communication.

Abstract and summary both condense information, but an abstract is attached to the writer's own academic work and follows a fixed pattern (purpose, method, findings, conclusion), while a summary can be written of any text by any reader to record its main ideas. Both must be accurate, concise, objective and written in the writer's own words.

Meeting documents follow a sequence: a notice announces the meeting (date, time, venue, purpose) and is circulated in advance; the agenda lists the items to be discussed in order; the minutes record what was discussed and decided. Minutes are approved at the next meeting and become an official record. Notices in general (for events, examinations, lost and found) must be short, clear and signed by an authorised person.

These forms of functional writing are essential in offices, colleges, NGOs, village councils and businesses. They help organisations communicate clearly, keep records and make decisions transparently.
The syllabus begins with themes and conventions of Elizabethan tragedy, including conventions of presentation and acting, action and speech, and character, identity and the performer's art.
Elizabethan drama depended strongly on actors, speech and theatrical convention rather than modern realistic stage technology. Performance practices shaped how characters and action were understood.
Tragic action commonly involves conflict, violence, ambition, revenge or moral crisis. Elevated and expressive speech, including blank verse, is central to the dramatic power of the period.
Kyd's play is a major revenge tragedy. The murder of Horatio and Hieronimo's search for justice drive a plot of grief, revenge, delay, madness and theatrical deception.
Faustus trades his soul for knowledge and power through a pact with Lucifer. The tragedy explores ambition, temptation, free will, repentance and the limits of human aspiration.
Macbeth's ambition is intensified by the witches' prophecies and Lady Macbeth's encouragement. His murder of Duncan begins a cycle of guilt, fear, violence and tyranny that leads to destruction.
Ambition is a central force in Macbeth's fall. Shakespeare shows how desire for power becomes destructive when separated from moral restraint.
The witches, prophecies and visions create a supernatural atmosphere, but the play also leaves Macbeth responsible for the choices he makes.

sections.title: Themes and Conventions of Elizabethan Tragedy

blocks.text:
The syllabus prescribes themes and conventions of Elizabethan tragedy through M. C. Bradbrook, including presentation and acting, action, speech and the performer's art. Elizabethan tragedy developed through theatrical conventions that relied strongly on language and performance.

Common tragic concerns include ambition, revenge, moral conflict, violence, identity and downfall. Blank verse and powerful dramatic speech gave the stage flexibility and emotional force.

Thomas Kyd's The Spanish Tragedy is a foundational revenge tragedy. Hieronimo's grief after Horatio's murder develops into a demand for justice in a world where ordinary institutions fail him.

The play uses delay, madness, revenge and a play-within-the-play. It helped establish conventions later associated with Elizabethan and Jacobean revenge drama.

Christopher Marlowe's Doctor Faustus presents a learned man dissatisfied with ordinary limits. Faustus makes a pact that promises extraordinary knowledge and power but places his soul in danger.

His tragedy develops through temptation, pride, fear and repeated opportunities to reconsider his choice. The play asks whether unlimited ambition can bring fulfilment and explores the tension between free will, sin and repentance.

Shakespeare's Macbeth presents the destruction caused by ambition and political murder. After hearing the witches' prophecies, Macbeth chooses to kill Duncan and seize the throne.

The crime produces guilt, suspicion and further violence. Lady Macbeth also suffers psychological collapse. The supernatural shapes the atmosphere and tempts interpretation, but Macbeth's choices remain central to his downfall. The play explores ambition, guilt, kingship, fate and moral responsibility.
The introductory unit is prescribed from A. K. Mehrotra's An Illustrated History of Indian Literature in English. The field includes Indian authors who use English across poetry, drama and fiction.

The poem transforms the casuarina tree into a symbol of memory and emotional attachment. The tree is connected with childhood, absent loved ones, nature and the desire to preserve memory through poetry.

sections.title: In the Zoo – A. K. Ramanujan

blocks.text: A prescribed poem by Ramanujan. Students should study its imagery, observation, voice and treatment of the human relationship with the zoo and its inhabitants from the assigned text.
The poem creates an image of absence and searching. Its compact imagery invites reflection on identity, loss and the difficulty of locating the self.

The poem describes a collective journey that begins with enthusiasm but gradually loses unity and purpose. It can be read as a reflection on idealism, conflict, disappointment and the meaning of pilgrimage.

The play presents a disturbing future in which poverty and global inequality turn the human body into a commodity. It explores exploitation, technology, consumer power and the unequal relationship between rich and poor societies.
Balram Halwai narrates his rise from poverty and servitude to entrepreneurship. The novel examines class inequality, corruption, ambition, violence and the darker side of economic change in India.

sections.title: Indian Writing in English: Background and Poetry

blocks.text:
The course introduces Indian Writing in English through A. K. Mehrotra and then moves across poetry, drama and fiction. The poetry unit includes Toru Dutt, A. K. Ramanujan, Jayanta Mahapatra and Nissim Ezekiel.

Our Casuarina Tree links nature with memory and loss. A Missing Person uses compressed imagery around absence and identity. Enterprise turns a journey into a reflection on idealism and disappointment. For Ramanujan's In the Zoo, students should base detailed interpretation on the prescribed poem.

Manjula Padmanabhan's Harvest imagines a world in which economically vulnerable people can be drawn into arrangements where their bodies become resources for wealthy outsiders.

The play uses technology and a futuristic situation to examine poverty, exploitation, global inequality and commodification. It asks what happens to dignity and autonomy when survival itself is controlled by economic power.

Aravind Adiga's The White Tiger is narrated by Balram Halwai, who describes his movement from poverty and servitude toward wealth and independence. His story exposes deep inequality between privileged and poor India.

Balram's success is morally complicated, making the novel more than a simple success story. Corruption, class, violence, ambition and economic transformation are central themes. The first-person narrative also forces readers to confront the narrator's own justification of his actions.
Androcentrism places male experience or perspective at the centre and treats it as the general norm.
Androgyny refers to the combination or crossing of characteristics conventionally labelled masculine and feminine.
Confessional writing uses personal experiences, emotions and private struggles as important literary material.
Feminism challenges gender inequality. The syllabus introduces first, second and third waves to show changing priorities and forms of feminist thought and activism.
Patriarchy is a social system in which men hold dominant power and authority in major institutions and relationships.
Gender refers to socially shaped roles and expectations associated with sex categories. Masculinities studies the different social forms through which manhood is constructed.
'The Other' describes people defined as different from a dominant norm. 'Subaltern' refers broadly to socially or politically marginalised groups with limited access to dominant power.
Gender stereotypes are fixed and simplified beliefs about how women and men are expected to behave.
The mirror speaks as an apparently exact observer while a woman confronts ageing and changing identity. The poem explores self-image, truth, time and anxiety about appearance.

sections.title: I'm Wife; I've Finished That – Emily Dickinson

blocks.text: Dickinson's poem examines the change in female identity associated with marriage. Its language questions the categories through which a woman's social position is defined.

sections.title: Little Red Cap – Carol Ann Duffy

blocks.text: Duffy rewrites the Little Red Riding Hood story from a female perspective. The poem links sexuality, literary apprenticeship, power and the development of an independent poetic voice.

The play examines women, career, power and the costs of success within unequal social structures. Marlene's professional achievement is placed beside the experiences of women from different historical and social positions.
The story centres on Dopdi Mejhen, an Adivasi woman subjected to state violence. Her final refusal to be shamed turns the violated body into an act of resistance.
The novel follows Celie's movement from abuse and silence toward independence, self-respect and supportive relationships. It explores race, gender, violence, sisterhood and empowerment.

The syllabus introduces androcentrism, androgyny, confessional mode, feminisms, patriarchy, gender, masculinities, the Other, subalternity and gender stereotypes. These concepts provide tools for understanding how literature represents gender and power.

They help students ask who has authority, whose experience is treated as normal, how social roles are constructed and how marginalised voices resist dominant expectations.

Sylvia Plath's Mirror explores ageing, self-image and the desire for truthful reflection. Emily Dickinson's I'm Wife; I've Finished That examines the shift in social identity created by marriage.

Carol Ann Duffy's Little Red Cap rewrites a familiar tale to present female sexual and artistic development. Together, the poems demonstrate different ways women poets question identity, gender expectations and the construction of female experience.

Caryl Churchill's Top Girls examines female success within structures shaped by class and gender. Its women come from different historical and social backgrounds, allowing the play to question whether individual achievement alone amounts to liberation.

Mahasweta Devi's Draupadi presents the extreme vulnerability of an Adivasi woman facing state violence. Dopdi's final resistance refuses the shame imposed upon her and transforms vulnerability into defiance.

Alice Walker's The Color Purple traces Celie's development from oppression and silence toward greater independence. Letters give her a means of expression while relationships with other women become important sources of strength.

The novel examines gender violence, racism, family, sexuality, sisterhood and self-respect. Celie's growing ability to speak, work and define herself makes empowerment a central theme.

The course studies literature from Commonwealth countries and focuses on cultural dilemmas, hegemony, exploitation and the effects of colonisation. Unit I prescribes Helen Tiffin's Commonwealth Literature: Comparison and Judgement.
Colonial rule can alter language, identity, institutions and cultural values. Commonwealth writing often examines how societies respond to these changes and negotiate inherited colonial structures.

sections.title: A Far Cry from Africa – Derek Walcott

blocks.text: Walcott's poem confronts colonial violence in Kenya while expressing the speaker's divided cultural loyalties. It explores violence, colonial history and the conflict of belonging to more than one cultural inheritance.
The Australian poem explores pregnancy and the intimate connection between woman and unborn child. It presents creation, bodily experience and maternal consciousness.
Curnow's poem examines questions of settlement, belonging and identity in New Zealand. It reflects tension between inherited European culture and the reality of life in another land.

sections.title: I Will Marry When I Want – Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o

blocks.text: The Kenyan play presents exploitation, class inequality and the continuing influence of colonial and capitalist power. The experiences of ordinary workers and peasants expose economic and social injustice.

Achebe's novel centres on Okonkwo and an Igbo community facing the arrival of British colonial rule and Christian missionaries. It explores tradition, masculinity, social change, cultural conflict and colonial disruption.

The syllabus introduces Commonwealth Literature through Helen Tiffin's discussion of comparison and judgement. The course does not claim that individual texts represent entire countries; instead, it uses selected works to explore hegemony, exploitation and cultural dilemmas associated with colonisation.

Students should therefore read the texts in their specific settings while also considering larger questions of colonial power, identity, language and adaptation.

Derek Walcott's A Far Cry from Africa presents colonial violence and a divided sense of cultural belonging. Judith Wright's Man to Woman turns to the intimate experience of pregnancy and creation. Allen Curnow's House and Land examines settlement and belonging in New Zealand.

These poems demonstrate the range of Commonwealth writing: political conflict, personal bodily experience and cultural identity can all become central literary concerns.

sections.title: I Will Marry When I Want

blocks.text:
Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o's I Will Marry When I Want examines Kenyan society through class conflict and exploitation. The play focuses on ordinary people whose lives remain shaped by unequal economic structures even after formal colonial rule.

It criticises the alliance of wealth, power and institutions that benefits elites while workers and peasants struggle. The drama therefore connects colonial history with continuing social and economic inequality.

Chinua Achebe's Things Fall Apart portrays Igbo life before and during the arrival of British colonial rule. Okonkwo is a respected but deeply rigid man whose personal fears and ideals of masculinity shape his actions.

The coming of missionaries and colonial administration creates divisions within the community and challenges established institutions. The novel explores tradition, change, masculinity, religion and colonial disruption while presenting African society with complexity rather than through colonial stereotypes.
